# Introduction to Advanced Navigation {#course-intro}

These course notes and this project are inspired by Roger Labbe's [Kalman Filtering and Bayesian Filters in Python](https://github.com/rlabbe/Kalman-and-Bayesian-Filters-in-Python/) in both content and structure. There are many great textbooks and resources on the theory of autonomous navigation, but there are fewer resources that pair the theory directly to practical implementations in an accessible programming language in such a way that Roger pairs Kalman filters with Python. This course and these notes are intended to fill that gap by providing a comprehensive introduction to advanced robot navigation techniques, including Kalman filters, particle filters, and other state estimation methods, and pairing this directly to practical implementations in Python.

This course was developed as part of the curriculum for Worcester Polytechnic Institute's Robotics Engineering program. The primary use case of these notes is for students in that program who are current (or former!) students!. That said, like Mr. Labbe's conribution, this is also for anyone interested in learning about advanced robot navigation techniques or teaching it. I too have stood on the shoulders of those who contributed to the open source literature before me, and this is my rung in the ladder. 

Previously this course was structured and integrated directly through Canvas, a learning management system used by many universities. However, I have since restructured the course materials to be hosted in a public GitHub repository for a variety of reasons. First and foremost is the simple availability of the materials and the ability for students to easily access and refer back to these materials as needed. Second, in April and May of 2026 there was a notable and widespread cyber attack on Canvas that rendered the platform inaccessible for several days...right at the end of the Spring semester grading period. As a simple reliability precaution, having the materials available from multiple sources is a simple way to ensure that students can always access the materials. Additionally, hosting the materials on GitHub allows for easier version control and collaboration rather than the significantly manual process of managing course materials on Canvas. Finally, there is a substantial amount of code that is associated with the course projects, and hosting the materials on GitHub allows for easier management of the code and the ability for students to fork the repository, engendering the development of good software development practices and the building of a code-based portfolio that students can show to potential employers.

## Why Write This Course? {#why-this-course}

The motivation for writing this course was a product of circumstance. After finishing up my Master's degree, I was looking for a job which lead me to an position with Penn State's Applied Research Laboratory and their Navigation Research and Development Division. I knew I liked working with autonomous mobile robots, but hadn't really settle on a specific topic. Throughout the interview process and the first couple of months on the job, I eventually settled in with navigation systems department. I found that, while I was working on the big navigation systems of submarines, to my surprise, it was all the same math! 

To a certain extent, this prompts a discussion of what is a machine versus a robot, and an autonomous vehicle... but that's best left for a lecture on philosophy. Suffice it to say, the modern roboticists writing the algorithms that we use borrowed heavily from the aerospace and maritime navigation communities, and the applications are nearly identical. The only real difference is the scale of the problem and the curvature of the Earth. This is reason enough to teach these things from a unified perspective, but the job I got when subsequently wrapping up my PhD was with an tech company making autonomous flying vehicles. What would have been traditionally termed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones were being made increasingly autonomous and therefore robotic. As such, this isn't so much a course on "robot navigation" as it is a course on how we get a computer system to understand where it is in the world through means of perceiving its environment (as opposed to through telecommunication and IP addressing). That computer system might inform a human pilot or navigator or it might serve to inform the autonomous control systems and decision making of a robot. Either way, the underlying mathematical techniques are the same.

This course delves into the sophisticated techniques and algorithms used by autonomous systems to navigate complex, real-world environments with precision and efficiency. Building upon fundamental concepts in robotics and navigation, this course equips students with advanced knowledge and practical skills necessary to develop cutting-edge navigation systems for autonomous robots operating in diverse scenarios. The curriculum begins with a review of foundational principles in robot perception and localization before examining modern techniques in nonlinear estimation, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), multi-sensor fusion, and inertial navigation. Students will deepen their understanding of these concepts through hands-on exercises and simulations. By the end of the course, students will have the ability to design, implement, and evaluate modern navigation systems for autonomous robots.

## How to Use the Foundations

The foundations part is a compact reference, not a second undergraduate degree in
mathematics. It establishes the shared language used by the rest of the book:
coordinate frames and attitude conventions, linear algebra, probability, and
reliable scientific Python. Read it before the first project if any of those
topics feel rusty, then return to the relevant chapter when an implementation
needs it. The examples use Python because it makes numerical ideas easy to test
and visualize; the conventions and algorithms carry directly to C++, Rust, and
other production languages.

## Recommended Prerequisites {#prerequisites}

To get the most out of this course, it is recommended that students have a solid understanding of the following topics. While there is some review of these topics in the foundations chapters, it is assumed that students have prior experience with these topics:

-   Intermediate knowledge of probability theory (conditional probability, probability distributions, etc.)
-   Intermediate knowledge of functional and/or object-oriented programming in a modern programming language such as Java, Python \>3.7, C17, C++11, Rust 1.90 or newer
-   Intermediate knowledge of linear algebra (matrix operations, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, etc.)
-   Knowledge of linear probabilistic estimation techniques (Bayes Filter, Kalman Filter)

This course is intended for graduate students with a background in robotics or a related field. It is intended for advanced first-year students (e.g. second semester master's students) or second-year graduate students in robotics, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, or computer science. Programming will also be a major component of this course. You should have experience with a modern programming language such as Python, Java, Rust, C, C++, or C#. Finally, you should have some knowledge of linear probabilistic estimation techniques such as the Bayes filter and the Kalman filter. If you are unfamiliar with any of these topics, you should review them before starting this course, as they will only be briefly reviewed in this course.

## Textbooks and Resources {#resources}

These notes are intended as a comprehensive *guide* to the material covered in this course and decidedly take a more practical approach than a traditional theoretical textbook. However, there are several textbooks that I would recommend as additional resources for students who want to learn more about the material covered in this course. These include:

-   *Probabilistic Robotics* by Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, and Dieter Fox
-   *Springer Handbook of Robotics* by Bruno Siciliano and Oussama Khatib
-   *Robotics, Vision and Control* by Peter Corke (recommend the 3rd edition which is Python based)
-   *Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python* by Roger Labbe (text and code, useful for both the theory and tutorials in Python)
-   *Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems* by Paul D. Groves

These course notes will be the primary source of information for the course. However, these references are highly recommended for further reading and understanding of the material.

While these references will not be required for completing the course (as in, I don’t assign homework problems from them) or in understanding the material contained within, they are all exceptionally good references written and edited by some of the leading contributors to robotics and autonomous navigation over the past thirty years.

I regularly refer to *Probabilistic Robotics* and it is a worthwhile purchase. If you are reading this as one of my students at WPI *Probabilistic Robotics* should be the only one you need to buy. *Springer Handbook of Robotics* and *Robotics, Vision and Control* can be downloaded as a PDF for free with your WPI credentials via the library. Additionally, *Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python* can be downloaded as a PDF free of charge. The readings for *Principles of GNSS* will be provided as needed as I only cover a few chapters of that book.

I would further suggest investing in getting a copy of all the books except *Principles of GNSS* as you will, have, or are going to get significant usage out of them. *Robotics, Vision and Control*, *Springer Handbook of Robotics*, and *Probabilistic Robotics* are all required or recommended references throughout the undergraduate and graduate WPI Robotics Engineering programs. So, if you don’t already have a copy of them, I suggest getting one. If, after this course, you find yourself interested in global scale (strategic, marine, or aerospace-grade) inertial navigation or getting a deeper understanding of GPS/GNSS specifically, then get a copy of *Principles of GNSS* and possibly *Strapdown Inertial Navigation Technology* by David Titterton and John Weston as these two references delve more into the aerospace and maritime navigation problems and satellite based radio navigation.

As this is intended as a graduate course, you should consider these notes and demonstrations (along with the corresponding lectures and slides) as the *minimum* amount of information you need to know to pass this course. If you wish to excel in this course and in graduate school in general, it is expected that you will read (or at least scan) and refer to the suggested readings. You do not have to read all of the suggested readings, nor do you necessarily have to take detailed notes on the readings. I assign multiple texts to get you various different presentations of the same material.

I would suggest approaching this course in one of the following ways, depending on what works best for you and your note-taking style.

1.  Read the suggested readings before the lecture to get a detailed, but verbose and hard to digest, presentation of the material and consider the lectures a more streamlined and easier to digest presentation to tie things together
2.  View the lectures first to ease into the material and then read the readings after the lecture to reinforce your understanding of the material
3.  Scan the readings first to get a general idea of the material, view the lectures, and then re-read the readings in detail to reinforce your understanding of the material

Again, these are merely suggestions. In general, it is a good practice to not necessarily memorize or take excessively detailed notes, but rather - especially given the project-based nature of this course - to understand where the information is in the readings and lectures so that you can refer to it while working through the projects. As we will get into in [About Me](#about-me), I have bounced back and forth between academia and industry several times, and one of the most important skills I have learned is how to quickly find the information I need in a textbook or reference manual, and I have rarely ever found myself in a situation where I did not have access to physical or digital reference materials and time to look up the answer.

## Module Roadmaps

| Part | Role in the course | Assessment status |
|---|---|---|
| Foundations | Shared conventions, numerical tools, and Python habits | Required background and reference |
| Sensing through Filtering | Module 1: construct and evaluate a visual-inertial estimator | Assessed |
| SLAM | Module 2: FastSLAM and data association | Assessed |
| Global Navigation | Module 3: loose INS/GNSS integration | Assessed |
| Practical and Advanced Topics | Production concerns, smoothing, receiver-level GNSS, and research directions | Enrichment only unless an assignment says otherwise |

## Code Conventions

Python blocks that execute during book rendering are **runnable examples** and
use deterministic inputs whenever they include randomness. Blocks marked
`eval: false` are **interface sketches**: they show the intended shape without
claiming a complete implementation. Blocks labelled as text or pseudocode specify
control flow and ownership, not executable code. This distinction is deliberate;
a concise model contract is often more useful than a deceptively incomplete
"complete system" listing.

## Course Philosophy {#course-philosophy}

The notion of a closed book timed exam as the epitome of technical academic assessment is an anachronism in the age of the internet and digital reference materials. Throughout your future career, you will almost always have access to reference materials and the ability to look up information as needed. The skill of quickly finding the information you need in a textbook or reference manual is a crucial one, and it is one that I have found to be more important than memorizing specific details. This is a skill that will serve you well in graduate school and in your career, so I encourage you to practice it in this course.

In a similar notion to my dislike of closed-book timed exams, I tend to view things like grades and homework assignments as similarly anachronistic and prefer a project-based approach to learning that produces tangible results and artifacts that students can use to demonstrate their understanding of the material and to build a portfolio of work that they can show to potential employers. This is a philosophy that I picked up from my wife's undergraduate experience in art school as part of a graphic design program. At some point, we had gotten into the discussion about worrying about grades and GPAs and she made the shocking point to me that she didn't look at her GPA or care about her grades. Instead, she focused on building a portfolio of work that she could show to potential employers. At the time, these were a physical thing (we've probably still got it somewhere in our attic or basement) that she would send samples of to jobs and take with her on interviews. This was a revelation to me as I had always been focused on grades and GPAs as the primary measure of success in my academic career.

This also rings true to graduate engineering education as well. While there are courses where grades will be considered your only measure of success, in general most graduate engineering programs will ask you to complete some sort of project or thesis at the masters level, and at the PhD level you are judged primarily on your published research and the impact of that research. These are tangible things that you can show to potential employers and that will be the primary measure of your success in your career. I have used such graduate school projects and research to land interviews and jobs. As such, this course will be entirely project-based, this material hosted on GitHub, and students are encouraged to fork the repository, clone it, and then use their solutions to the projects as part of their portfolio of work that they can show to potential employers.

### Grading and Project Submission {#grading}

Course grading will follow the standard A-F scale. Course incompletes and/or extensions will only be given in extreme circumstances and must be requested in writing prior to the end of the semester. As the online program is designed to be more flexible than a traditional on-campus program, I understand that many students are working full-time jobs, have families, and are juggling many other responsibilities. I too worked full time throughout graduate school. As such I understand that sometimes things come up and you may need more time to complete a project. If you are facing such a situation, please reach out in writing to request an extension *prior to the end of the semester*.

Ultimately, the goal of this course is to learn the material and to be able to apply it in practice. Deadlines are important, but they are never nearly as tight as they are in a traditional course with a closed-book timed exam. As such, ultimately all projects are due by the end of the semester, and students are encouraged to submit their work for feedback as early as possible. "Deadlines" and "Due dates" posted for projects are more of a guideline to help students stay on track and to ensure that they are making progress throughout the semester. However, if you need more time to complete a project, you can submit it for feedback as late as the end of the semester. I will provide feedback on all projects submitted by the end of the semester, but I encourage you to submit your work for feedback as early as possible so that you can get feedback and make improvements before the end of the semester.

My philosophy on grading is centered around the Robotics Engineering [PhD Technical qualifier](https://www.wpi.edu/sites/default/files/RBE-PhD-Handbook_.pdf) and a project-based curriculum where an average grade of roughly a B+ (two A’s and one B) is used to demonstrate expertise and pass the qualifier. I similarly grade assignments based on the following ratings: Excellent, Acceptable, Marginal, and Unacceptable, with details of what qualifications each level requires. I generally try to structure assignments such that an Acceptable rating corresponds to a B.

### Project Guidance {#project-guidance}

This course is primarily about the theory of navigation. However, as engineers, our goal is to provide some sort of useful technology. While much of the theoretical content in this course will be presented as applied mathematics, demonstration of understanding will require a practical implementation in a computer programming language. As this is an advanced course, it is expected that you will come into this course with an intermediate ability to program in a modern version of a language such as C17, C++17, or Python 3.9 or newer versions. Minor debugging help will not be provided on a one-on-one basis. Please post questions, concerns, comments, et cetera on the appropriate discussion boards to receive help.

Each project will require a write-up/report plus submission of your code. Students are free to select the programming language of their choice. Write ups and reports should resemble an academic research paper.

While students are permitted to complete the assignments in any programming language that they prefer (the main deliverable is the report, which should include figures, thus the suggestion towards Python), generally, robotics and autonomous systems use a mixture of Python, C, and C++, with some growing interest in Rust. As such, any code demonstrations will be given in Python. While I am personally proficient in Python, C++, and Rust, I will only provide programming support/debugging in Python as the starter code in this course is in Python.

I am also proficient in Matlab; however, I strongly advise [against](https://www.rath.org/matlab-is-a-terrible-programming-language.html) using [Matlab](https://www.quora.com/Why-is-MATLAB-so-bad) for a variety of [technical](https://web.archive.org/web/20140603062443/http://abandonmatlab.wordpress.com/2009/07/) and [ethical](https://metarabbit.wordpress.com/2013/10/18/why-python-is-better-than-matlab-for-scientific-software/) reasons, and the fact that generally speaking just about anything Matlab can do, Python can do equally well, if not better, and for free. If you ask me for help in debugging Matlab code, my first suggestion will be to re-write it in Python. While I will accept coded submissions written in Matlab (again, the point is to *apply the math* not to *learn to code*), suffice it to say, Python, C, and C++ are the most common languages used in the robotics and autonomous systems industry, as well as in the related industries of data science and machine learning, and it would be to your benefit to practice in one or more of those languages.

Based on past submissions here is some general guidance. First, take anything that is in the project description as given. You do not need to re-write this as your introduction outside of any specific choices you might make regarding methodology (some assignments permit students to choose which algorithm to implement). Second, I prefer a single-column format. I grade your papers online via Canvas, and while IEEE is the predominant publisher in the robotics and aerospace field, their two-column format is tough to read on the built in PDF viewer in Canvas and it can also do weird things with figure placement and make figures illegibly small. Third, write things out like a research report. This means limited use of bullet points, and do not just get a chatbot to spit things out for you. This is not an anti-AI stance or chatbot ban — we'll get to that in [AI Policy and Software Dependencies](#ai-policy-and-dependencies) — but what I am looking to assess you on is your actual understanding of the material. The classic bulleted list of: “some short text – a longer and more detailed explanation of the thing” for every single section is a dead giveaway that you're using a chatbot to write your report. Using a chatbot to write your report is an indicator that you are not fully engaging with and digesting the material.

Finally, as a general format here is what I am expecting. Treat this as general guidance in addition to the specific rubric deliverables for each project. You do not have to follow this format, but it is a good starting point for structuring your report.

1.  **Introduction**: briefly summarize and contextualize the assignment. Do not restate the project description. (1-2 paragraphs)
2.  **Methods**: tell me how and why you solved or attempted to solve the problem(s) and deliverables posed by the assignment including a brief discussion of your code (3-5 paragraphs depending on what is asked for)
3.  **Results**: *present* your results. Discuss why these metrics are useful metrics to look at if that adds clarity (several paragraphs, figures, and/or tables)
4.  **Discussion**: *talk* about your results. Note any interesting findings. Critique the results. Contrast different methods if applicable (3-5 paragraphs)
5.  **Conclusion**: briefly summarize your report and wrap it up. (1 long paragraph max)

Note, this is approximately 15-20 paragraphs, which is about 3-5 pages of text depending on paragraph length and figure placement. I do not need a 20-page highly detailed thesis, nor do I want a 1-page report with one sentence answers to questions and some pictures. I am looking for something in between that demonstrates your understanding of the material and your ability to communicate that understanding effectively in writing. Some things to consider when writing your report in addition to the specific deliverables asked for in the rubric are:

-   What problem are you solving?
-   Why is it important?
-   What is your approach?
-   What are your results?
-   What are the limitations of your approach?
-   What are the next steps?
-   What did you learn?
-   What may have gone wrong?

### Code style guide {#code-style-guide}

While programming is not the primary concern of this course, it is nonetheless a major component and will be graded as part of your overall assessment, predominantly to serve as an anti-plagiarism mechanism and make sure you did the work yourself. I suggest that you adopt the following style guide principles for your work in this course and any other programming assignments you might encounter. This policy should assist you in debugging your code when errors arise, assist with presenting your work in an acceptable manner and help you pick up where you left off the day before when working on an assignment. To borrow a philosophy from [Google’s C++ style guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html): most code will be read more often than it is written so having clear, concise, well written, and well documented code is essential.

#### Code Documentation, Comments, and Readability

-   All code should be well-documented and include inline comments explaining the purpose of functions, methods, and complex logic.
-   Document the input parameters, output values, and a brief description of the purpose for each function, method, and class.
-   Use descriptive variable and function names that convey their purpose or functionality.
-   Comment sections of code that may be non-intuitive or involve complex algorithms.
-   Maintain consistent indentation throughout the code.

#### Modular Design and Debugging

-   Break down complex tasks into modular functions or methods.
-   Strive for a clean separation of concerns in your code structure.
-   Implement appropriate error handling using try-except blocks where necessary.
-   Provide meaningful error messages that aid in identifying and resolving issues.
-   Consider writing unit tests to ensure that code is behaving correctly.

#### Version Control and Submission

-   Use a version control system (e.g., Git) to track changes and manage your codebase.
-   Use a public repo database (e.g. GitHub) to store and build a code-based portfolio.
-   Submit your assignments through the designated submission channel on Canvas.
-   Submit each file individually (e.g., Python scripts, report pdf, Jupyter notebooks, etc.) and do not compress them into a single archive.

Some additional references:

-   [Google's Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html) sections 3.2-3.4, 3.8, 3.1 and 3.16-3.18

-   [PEP 8 – Style Guide for Python Code](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/)

-   [The Hitchhikers Guide to Python Coding Style](https://docs.python-guide.org/writing/style/)

### AI Policy and Software Dependencies {#ai-policy-and-dependencies}

When I first started teaching this course things like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot and other such chatbots and coding agents had just been introduced and were not nearly as widely used as they are now. I used to note that, while these tools were interesting and helpful with getting some of the more mundane programming tasks done, they were not yet at a level where they could be used to do your projects for you.

Three years later, they're good enough to do your homework projects for you now.

Furthermore, I do not want to be hypocritical and say that you can’t use these tools when I myself use them all the time to assist with programming tasks. I am even using them now to help me write the contents of this course, and in my day job as a navigation engineer writing code that is used in production on real robots and vehicles, I use these tools all the time to assist with programming tasks.

However, they are still fundamentally functionally junior partners. While very capable of doing now complex engineering tasks, they do still require that you check their work. For you to be able to check their work, you need to understand the material and be able to read and understand the code that they produce. If you can’t do that, then you can’t use these tools effectively. If you can do that, then these tools can be very helpful in assisting with programming tasks. They can be particularly helpful in building code blocks and prototyping code when you’re unsure of how to do something. However, they won’t be able to do your projects *entirely* for you as part of the deliverables for each project is demonstrating *your* understanding and application of the material.

To that end, the use of AI in this course is not banned, and in fact I encourage students to thoughtfully use AI to assist with their programming, and there are no limitations to what software packages students can use. There is one specific caveat to this, which is the `filterpy` package or other such packages that have pre-built implementations of the *filtering* algorithms that we will be implementing in this course. The use of such packages is not *banned*. In general students can expect a passing 'C' grade for code that runs, produces the required output, and has a written report. To receive a higher grade, students will need to demonstrate a deeper understanding. Implementing the filter predict and update steps without relying on a filtering or state estimation library (e.g. using linear algebra libraries like `numpy`/`scipy` only), or your report contains a detailed section that walks through the mathematics of your implementation and explains every design decision — state vector choices, model assumptions, covariance initialization — in enough detail that someone could reproduce your work from your description alone even if you use `filterpy`. Keep in mind, that the level of detail required for a 'B' when using `filterpy` will be much higher than the level of detail required for a 'B' if you implement the filter yourself.
